messages.subject: The inner workings of simulations in S Plus: How can we improve efficiency?
messages.subject_clean: The inner workings of simulations in S Plus: How can we improve efficiency?
messages.body_plain:
Hello All,

I was wondering if someone could conceptually explain how S Plus uses
memory when simulations are run.  I do a great deal of simulation work,
but I do not have a firm grasp of what S Plus is doing "behind the
scenes."  For example, if I run a simulation that has, say, 1000
generations/replications and it takes an hour, it may take 3 or 4 if I
double the generations/replications to 2000.  It seems as you increase
the generations/replications the computing time needed grows
exponentially.  I have also been building simulations where there are
multiple loops.  This seems to really take a huge amount of time to
complete.  It is not a good idea to build several loops in big
simulation programs?

I think there may be a way to refresh the memory after each loop, but
I'm not sure how to do it or if it would reduce the amount of computer
time?

Usually I use S Plus 2000 on a Windows with a 1ghz processor and 512mb
or ram with good success.  I have, however, been talked into using
machines that are billed as "high performance" and cost a ton of money
each year.  But, I've been ending up with messages such as the following
(I think these high performance machines run S Plus 5 in a Unix
environment):

Problem in summary.lm(lm(Standardized.X[, 1] ~ Stand..: Unable to obtain
requested dynamic memory
Error during wrapup: Unable to obtain requested dynamic memory
logout

Am I just simply asking S Plus to do too much?  I have tried to rid my
code of wasted statements and thus reduce time, so, I don't think it is
because my code is sloppy?

Is it a good idea to increase the amount of memory S Plus uses, and if
so, any recommendations?  What does this really do anyway?

In a loop is it better to do several things together or to do them on
separate lines, or does it really even matter?  A trivial example that
illustrates the question may be something like the following::

a <- lm(Y ~ X)
sum.a <- summary(a)
c.a <- coef(sum.a)
b <- c.a[1,2]

or all at once as:

b <- coef(summary(lm(Y~X)))[1,2]

To save computing time, is one strategy better than the other?
I've been told that R is "more efficient" at doing simulations because
of the way it handles memory issues.  I'm not sure if this is true, but,
just a question I was interested in finding out the answer to.

Anyway, thanks and any advice on the inner workings of S Plus with
regards to simulations and efficient computing would be greatly
appreciated (sorry for the long rambling message).
Take Care,
Ken

messages.body_plain:
It's hard to answer such questions in generality.  Bill Venables and I
devoted a chapter of `S Programming' to such issues for several reasons,
including

a) What's a good way to do a task often depends on whether you are using
S3, S4 or R.

b) Which system is most efficient depends on the task.

There's a lot of distilled wisdom (Bill's, of course) there and I commend
it to you.

But for independent simulations, there is (normally) no good reason why the
time should not be linear with little memory growth.  S-PLUS 6.0 and R are
both better at that than S3-based systems (such as S-PLUS 2000), but I have
never yet seen a simulation problem where memory build-up could not be
avoid in S-PLUS 3.4/2000.  If all else fails, use the equivalent of For()
and unroll the loop so the simulations are separate top-level calls.
(See the examples in the reference above.)

Brian Ripley

When I try to run this as testfx(AGE), where AGE is one of the columns of
test.data, I get an error that the variable x cannot be found.  I have tried
about 30 variants on the above, trying to get the function to understand
that x is one of the parameters, and that the function is supposed to
substitute for it the value in the function call, but alas nothing works. 

(If I write testfx<-function(x) {answer<-someother.variable+x}, the system
seems to understand me perfectly.)

What am I doing wrong?  How do I get the parameter substituted into the
model statement?

Many thanks for your help.

Larry Hunsicker

messages.subject: Re: Query: Regression coeff
messages.body_plain:
> 
> I run a regression model and get the results into a results variable, but
> it just prints a report. What I would like to have are the individual
> elements of the regression outputs like betas, tstat, r squareds etc. Is
> there a way to get it into a structure which can then be used by something
> else to store those values for later use.

Try this complete example:

set.seed(104)
tmp.df <- data.frame(x1=rep(c("-","+"),each=4),
                     x2=rep(c("-","+"),each=2,times=2),
                     y=rnorm(8))
tmp.lm <- lm(y~x1*x2,data=tmp.df)
tmp.summary <- summary(tmp.lm)

# table of coef, stderr, t, and p-value
tmp.summary$coefficients

# just the coefficients
coefficients(tmp.lm)
# just the standard errors
sqrt(diag(tmp.summary$cov.unscaled))*tmp.summary$sigma
# r-squared value
tmp.summary$r.squared

Look at the summary.lm method for more goodies.

Sundar

messages.body_plain:
Dear S-News;
I do not understand the na.strings option of data.frame.  I have a matrix of
numbers (called reg) which is being generated within a piece of code.  The
matrix contains NA's, but these are not factors, nor is the matrix viewed as
anything other than numercial as a result of their presence;  e.g

summary(reg)
   Min. 1st Qu. Median    Mean 3rd Qu. Max. NA's 
 -5.736  -1.384      0 -0.2608  0.5966  6.1  291

For convenience, I want         to create a data frame and attach text
labels using cbind, i.e 

out <- data.frame(cbind(labs, reg))

But after this operation, the columns of reg have become factors and in
spite of the fact that the mode remains numeric;

mode(out$column4)
>"numeric"

the contents of reg, now list components of "out", are text.  I can fix this
by brute force by applying as.vector() to each column individually (which
changes the mode to "character") and the coercing the mode back to
"numeric", but this is awkward.  A proper fix, it seems, should involve the
na.strings option in data.frame(), but the help file doesn't describe any
options other than the default.   Any suggestions?  I'm using S-Plus 2000
for windows.
Thanks in advance,
Sean Keenan

messages.subject: Re: na.strings in data.frame()
messages.body_plain:
Sean,

  Here's what I think is going on. I may be way off.
> 
> out <- data.frame(cbind(labs, reg))

If reg is a numeric matrix, cbind(labs,reg) will return a matrix. Since
a matrix can only be one data type, reg will be converted to character.
See this example:

# BEGIN EXAMPLE #
col <- matrix(c(rnorm(20),rep(NA,10)),ncol=1)
lab <- c(rep("normal",20),letters[1:10])
out <- data.frame(cbind(lab,col))

> sapply(out, mode)
       lab      X1.2 
 "numeric" "numeric"
> sapply(out, data.class)
      lab     X1.2 
 "factor" "factor"
# END EXAMPLE #

Now here's the fix:

# BEGIN FIX #
col <- matrix(c(rnorm(20),rep(NA,10)),ncol=1)
lab <- c(rep("normal",20),letters[1:10])
out <- data.frame(lab,col)

> sapply(out, mode)
       lab       col 
 "numeric" "numeric"
> sapply(out, data.class)
      lab       col 
 "factor" "numeric"
# END FIX #

mode(out[,lab]) returns "numeric" because lab is of type "factor". I
usually use data.class to determine type.

Sundar

messages.body_plain:
I need to transfer large amounts of data from another program to Splus. I 
have been using tab separated ascii files, but it is somewhat slow to write 
and read the files (the files can be 10's of megs). Most of the data is 
floating point numbers, so I was wondering if it would be better to 
transfer via a binary file.

> I need to transfer large amounts of data from another program to Splus. I

> and read the files (the files can be 10's of megs). Most of the data is
> floating point numbers, so I was wondering if it would be better to

> minimum.  Column names and integer data would be nice too, but if necessary

Why not use connections via readMapped or readRaw?  (They need S-PLUS 5 or
6, of course.)   One can read almost any binary file that way, and
you get to choose the format.  I doubt if any way of reading the file will
be fast unless there are large chunks of the same format, e.g. large
blocks of doubles.  So one would want to write a dataframe by column, not
by row, for example.

My experience with this is entirely on Unix, but it looks like it is

messages.subject: Re: contrasts in Manova
messages.body_plain:
A few days ago, I asked a question about contrasts in Manova (see message 
below). Yuelin Li, Brian D. Ripley and someone from Insightful technical 
support answered. Following (I believe) Prof Ripley's suggestion, and 
restricting myself to the orthgonal contrasts defined for each factor, I 
slightly changed the code of summary.manova by (see diff below)
(*) adding an argument allsplit to tell wether to split factors or not
(*) if allsplit=T, asgn is changed to have only one element per test => each 
element is one of the predefined contrast.

bash-2.04$ diff summary.manova.ssc summary.m2.ssc 
1,2c1,2
< summary.manova <-
< function(object, univariate = F, test = "pillai", intercept = F)
---
>  summary.m2 <-
> function(object, allsplit=F, univariate = F, test = "pillai", intercept = F)
60c60,66
<               asgn <- object$assign
---
>           if (!allsplit)
>             asgn <-  object$assign
>           else
>             {
>               asgn <-  as.list(as.data.frame(t(unlist(object$assign))))
>               names(asgn) <- dimnames(object$effect)[[1]][1:length(asgn)]
>             }

Thus if allsplit=F, the summary is the same as for summary.manova, but if 
allsplit=T, each contrast is tested instead (see example below). This is a 
quick and durty work-around, but if anybody can tell me wether it is correct 
(within its range of applicability) or not, ie wether the given p-value tests 
the corresponding contrast, I would appreciate very much. The "new" function is 
attached.

> wafer.manova <- manova(cbind(pre.mean, post.mean) ~ spinsp, wafer)

> summary.m2(wafer.manova)
          Df Pillai Trace approx. F num df    den df    P-value 
   spinsp 2  0.24276       1.0361         4        30   0.40493
Residuals 15       
                                            
> summary.m2(wafer.manova, allsplit=T)
          Df Pillai Trace approx. F num df    den df    P-value 
 spinsp.L 1  0.20142      1.76554         2        14   0.20713
 spinsp.Q 1  0.04349      0.31828         2        14   0.73253
Residuals 15                                                   

Olivier

>Hi,

>Although I can define contrasts for a factor in manova (menu or commands), and 
>although it seems that the contrasts are registered in the manova object, I 
>cannot obtain the tests for the contrasts in the anova-table, since there are 
>no "split" argument in summary.manova. Is there an other way to obtain these 
>tests or an easy fix-around?
>
>thanks
>Olivier
>
>
>> version
>Professional Edition Version 6.0.2 Release 1 for Microsoft Windows : 2001
>> hatt4.maov <- manova (cbind(pp1,ple1)~group , data=hatt4)
>> summary(hatt4.maov)
>          Df Pillai Trace approx. F num df    den df    P-value
>    group 3  0.4876       7.7368         6       144         0
>Residuals 72
>> summary(hatt4.maov, split=list(group=list(C1=1,C2=2,C3=3)))
>Problem in summary: argument split= not matched: summary(hatt4.maov, split =
>li
>st(group = list(C1 = 1, C2 = 2, C3 = 3)))
>Use traceback() to see the call stack
>> args(summary.manova)
>function(object, univariate = F, test = "pillai", intercept = F)
>> args(summary.aov)
>function(object, intercept = F, split, expand.split = T, ssType = 1, ...)
>
>
>Faculty of Psychology and Education      Olivier.Renaud at pse.unige.ch
>University of Geneva    - 40, Bd du Pont d'Arve -   CH-1211 Geneva 4
>Tel: +41 22 705 9104  http://www.unige.ch/fapse/PSY/persons/prof-ana
 summary.m2 <-
function(object, allsplit=F, univariate = F, test = "pillai", intercept = F)
{
        manova.stats <- function(eig, q, df.res)
        {
                ans <- array(NA, c(4, 5))
                ans[, 1] <- c(sum(eig/(1 + eig)), prod(1/(1 + eig)), sum(eig), 
max(eig))
                p <- length(eig)
                s <- min(c(p, q))
                n <- 0.5 * (df.res - p - 1)
                m <- 0.5 * (abs(p - q) - 1)
                #
                #
                # pillai
                test <- ans[1, 1]
                tmp1 <- 2 * m + s + 1
                tmp2 <- 2 * n + s + 1
                ans[1, 2] <- (tmp2/tmp1 * test)/(s - test)
                ans[1, 3:4] <- s * c(tmp1, tmp2)
                #
                #
                # Hotelling-Lawley
                test <- ans[3, 1]
                tmp2 <- 2 * (s * n + 1)
                ans[3, 2] <- (tmp2 * test)/s/s/tmp1
                ans[3, 3:4] <- c(s * tmp1, tmp2)
                #
                #
                # wilks
                test <- ans[2, 1]
                tmp1 <- df.res - 0.5 * (p - q + 1)
                tmp2 <- (p * q - 2)/4
                tmp3 <- p * p + q * q - 5
                if(tmp3 > 0)
                        tmp3 <- sqrt((p * p * q * q - 4)/tmp3)
                else tmp3 <- 1
                ans[2, 2] <- ((test^(-1/tmp3) - 1) * (tmp1 * tmp3 - 2 * 
tmp2))/p/q
                ans[2, 3:4] <- c(p * q, tmp1 * tmp3 - 2 * tmp2)
                #
                #
                # Roy's Max root (lower bound on p-value)
                test <- ans[4, 1]
                tmp1 <- max(c(p, q))
                tmp2 <- df.res - tmp1 + q
                ans[4, 2:4] <- c((tmp2 * test)/tmp1, tmp1, tmp2)
                #
                #
                # finally
                good <- ans[, 2] >= 0 & ans[, 3] > 0 & ans[, 4] > 0
                ans[good, 5] <- 1 - pf(ans[good, 2], ans[good, 3], ans[good, 4])
                ans
        }
        if(!inherits(object, "maov"))
                stop("object must be of class \"manova\" or \"maov\"")
        if(univariate)
                return(summary.mlm(object, intercept = intercept))
        effects <- object$effects
        asgn <- object$R.assign
        if(is.null(asgn))
          if (!allsplit)
            asgn <-  object$assign
          else
            {
              asgn <-  as.list(as.data.frame(t(unlist(object$assign))))
              names(asgn) <- dimnames(object$effect)[[1]][1:length(asgn)]
            }
        resid <- object$residuals
        wt <- object$weights
        if(!is.null(wt))
                resid <- resid * wt^0.5
        if(is.null(effects)) {
                df <- nterms <- neff <- 0
                ms <- alleff <- numeric(0)
                ss <- list()
                rl <- character(0)
        }
        else {
                nterms <- length(asgn)
                nobs <- dim(resid)[1]
                q <- dim(resid)[2]
                rl <- names(asgn)
                alleff <- unlist(asgn)
                neff <- length(alleff)
                if(!intercept && neff && rl[1] == "(Intercept)") {
                        asgn <- asgn[-1]
                        rl <- rl[-1]
                        nterms <- nterms - 1
                        nobs <- nobs - 1
                }
                ss <- vector("list", nterms)
                df <- numeric(nterms)
                if(nterms)
                        for(i in 1:nterms) {
                                ai <- asgn[[i]]
                                df[i] <- length(ai)
                                ss[[i]] <- crossprod(effects[ai,  , drop = F])
                        }
        }
        df.res <- object$df.resid
        if(is.null(df.res))
                df.res <- nobs - length(unlist(asgn))
        if(df.res > 0) {
                nterms <- nterms + 1
                df[nterms] <- df.res
                ss[[nterms]] <- crossprod(resid)
                rl[nterms] <- "Residuals"
                rss.qr <- qr(ss[[nterms]])
                ok <- df[ - nterms] > 0
                eigs <- array(NA, c(nterms - 1, q))
                stats <- array(NA, c(nterms - 1, 4, 5), list(rl[ - nterms], 
c("pillai",
                        "wilks lambda", "hotelling-lawley", "roy largest"), 
c("Statistic",
                        "approx. F", "num df   ", "den df   ", "P-value")))
                if(!is.null(rss.qr))
                        for(i in (1:(nterms - 1))[ok]) {
                                tmp <- Re(eigen(qr.coef(rss.qr, ss[[i]]), 
symmetric = F)$
                                        values)
                                eigs[i,  ] <- tmp
                                stats[i,  ,  ] <- manova.stats(tmp, df[i], 
df[nterms])
                        }
                names(ss) <- rl
                x <- list(row.names = rl, SS = ss, Df = df, Eigen.values = 
eigs, Stats = 
                        stats, test = test)
        }
        else {
                names(ss) <- rl
                x <- list(row.names = rl, Df = df, SS = ss)
        }
        oldClass(x) <- "summary.manova"
        x
}

messages.body_plain:
S-PLUS 6 R2 Windows XP

I have a question that may have to be answered by an Insightful developer.  I 
have a bunch of Weibull distribution paramters - scale, mu, and shape - 
calculated using weibullRob() in the robust library.  I also have the simple 
equation (sans the location parameter) used to relate mu and scale to shape:

mu/scale = gamma((shape+1)/shape)

The shape values that S-PLUS calculated for my data range from 1.73 to 10.3.  
As an aside exploratory analysis, I created a sequence of numbers with the 
command seq(1,15,.0001), then used these numbers as the shape value in the 
above equation to calculate the mu/scale ratio.  I plotted the ratio values vs 
the shape values in the sequence, and found that there are exactly 2 shape 
parameter values for each ratio except at the minimum ratio value 
(~0.8856031944) at the shape value of ~2.1662.

I would like to know how S-PLUS determines what the shape parameter should be.  
For instance, in my data when the shape paramter is 10.3, the mu/scale ratio is 
.95253.  This is the same as the ratio value for the shape value of 1.466.  Why 
would S-PLUS choose 10.3 over 1.466?

I need to know this because I need to estimate some shape paramters, and it 
would help to know how S-PLUS distinguishes between the values.  Thanks.

messages.subject: non-parametric t-test OR re-sampling
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have 18 samples (tissues) obtained from three different classes A, B,
C (6 samples for each class). For each sample I measured 4000 genes.

                      Class A            Class B        Class C
gene 1          1 2 3 4 5 6       1 2 3 4 5 6   1 2 3 4 5 6
gene 2
  :
gene 4000

Given the limited number of measurments for each class, it is difficult
to determine if these are normally distributed. Furthermore, the
variance within a single class is large for a number of genes.

Now I want to find out if which genes are are statistically different
between the classes. Thus for each individual gene I want to compare A
to B, A to C and B to C.

I'm aware of the existence of several non-parametric (t-tests) which
could be used to deal with this problem, but I'm not sure which one to
use.

As an alternative approach I thought it should be possible to persue
some kind of re-sampling procedure to test if
the observed difference is significant when compared to the distribution
of differences obtained from re-sampling.

Therefore, I have two questions:
1) what non-parametric test could I use?
2) How would a re-sampling approach look like for this situation?

Any help is appreciated

Antoine van Kampen

messages.subject: S & R list virus warning
messages.body_plain:
It appears that someone has harvested email addresses from the S-news or
one of the R lists and is sending out viruses. The mail does not come
from the lists, but appears to come from people on these lists. (Closer
examination of the headers indicates that it does not really come from
the person indicated in the "from" field.) The mail is probably directed
to people on these lists as well as others. I have received at least
three already. The most recent one has the subject line "Introduction on
ADSL" and a previous one had the subject line "A good tool".

The messages are infected with the WORM_KLEZ.G virus in an attachment.

I am not sure what mechanisms can be used to deter spammers from
harvesting email addresses from lists, but something should be
considered. One thing I know people have tried is to put blanks or other
characters into the publicly displayed addresses on  lists. This means
that people can read the lists and figure out an email address, but
simple automatic tools are foiled. Another possibility is to not make
the addresses  available.

I realize I can ask that my name be hidden on the list, but that breaks
the original intent of having names available: to be able to know who
else is involved in the list community.

Paul Gilbert

messages.body_plain:
Dear S+ users,

Next code shows that function "contour" with "save=T" and "plot=F" does not
behave correctly (at least under S+2000 / W98):

        > cell <- matrix(seq(0, 2, length = 4), ncol = 2)

        # 1. Correct behaviour (plot contour while computing contour line):
        > x <- c(2, 3)
        > y <- c(2, 3)
        > w1 <- contour(x, y, cell, levels = 1, save = T, plot = T)
                # number of points along contour line:
        > unlist(lapply(w1, function(cont.line) length(cont.line$x)))
         1 
         3

        # 2. Incorrect behaviour (DO NOT plot contour while computing
contour line AND change x and y values):
        > x <- c(0, 1)
        > y <- c(0, 1)  
        > w2 <- contour(x, y, cell, levels = 1, save = T, plot = F)
                # number of points along contour line:
        > unlist(lapply(w2, function(cont.line) length(cont.line$x)))
         1 
         0

Changing x and / or y should not change the number of points along the
contour line contrary to what is observed here: 3 points in the first case
(including one pair of NA's) and 0 point in the second.
This problem desappears if "contour" is always called with "plot=T". This
means that "contour" cannot be used in cases where plotting is not desired.
Is there any turnaround available? Is it possible for example to plot on a
NULL device?

Thank you for any help.

messages.subject_clean: Summary: running all models with 3 or less variables
messages.body_plain:
Hello All,

Thanks to Peter Ellis, Andrew Beckerman and especially Renaud Lancelot for
their suggestions.  I ended up using the suggestion offered by Renaud to
solve my problems.  He sent a script for function called combinations ( ),
along with guidance on how to change all the possible combinations of
integers to a model formula.  I had to make some changes since I was
interested in all models with 3, 2, 1 and 0 explanatory variables.  I don't
think what I have come up with is elegant, but it solves the problem
(especially since the sample size is small).  I had to alter the code
somewhat because I was interested in the resulting AIC values, but these
had to be adjusted to the AICc (small sample size AIC) values.  I am
attaching my script and the original email sent to me by Renaud.  Hopefully
I will be able to clean up the script to make it more generally applicable,
but I guess I'll have to see what time and my limited skills allow.  Thanks
for the help, Niels

combinations <- function(n, k)
{
# Compute all n choose k combinations of size k from 1:n
# Return matrix with k rows and choose(n,k) columns.
      if(!is.numeric(n) || length(n) != 1 || n %%
           1) stop("'n' must be an integer")
      if(!is.numeric(k) || length(k) != 1 || k %%
           1)
           stop("'k' must be an integer")
      if(k > n || k <= 0)
           return(numeric(0))
      rowMatrix <- function(n)
      structure(1:n, dim = c(1, n))
      colMatrix <- function(n)
      structure(1:n, dim = c(n, 1))
      if(k == n)
           return(colMatrix(n))
      if(k == 1)
           return(rowMatrix(n))
      L <- vector("list", k)
      # L[[j]] will contain combinations(N, j) for N = 2:n
      L[[1]] <- rowMatrix(2)
      L[[2]] <- colMatrix(2)
      Diff <- n - k
      for(N in seq(3, n, by = 1)) {
# loop over j in reverse order, to avoid overwriting
           for(j in seq(pmin(k, N - 1), pmax(
                2, N - Diff), by = -1))
                L[[j]] <- cbind(L[[j]],
                     rbind(L[[j - 1]],
                     N, deparse.level
                      = 0))
           if(N <= Diff + 1)
                L[[1]] <- rowMatrix(N)
           else L[[N - (Diff + 1)]] <-
                     numeric(0)
           if(N <= k)
                L[[N]] <- colMatrix(N)
      }
      L[[k]]
}
n <- 7
# n is the number of variables
k <- 3
# max number of parameters in models
resp <- L1000Wet[, "AMMA.abun"]
# response variable defined
X1 <- L1000Wet[, "RACA.Breed"]
X2 <- L1000Wet[, "L1000.Forest"]
X3 <- L1000Wet[, "Fish.Pres"]
X4 <- L1000Wet[, "Permanent"]
X5 <- L1000Wet[, "RLScaled1000"]
X6 <- L1000Wet[, "Shallow"]
X7 <- L1000Wet[, "EM.nonphal"]
# explanatory variables X1 through X7 defined
sample.size <- length (L1000Wet[[1]])
expl <- paste ("X", 1:n, sep = "")
# list of explanatory variables
out1 <- matrix (nrow = 64, ncol = 3, dimnames = list(paste ("fm", 1:64, sep
   = ""), c("resid DF", "Model DF", "AICc")))
out2 <- matrix (nrow = 64, ncol = 1, dimnames = list(paste ("fm", 1:64, sep
   = ""), c("Formula")))
#matrices for output - later put in data frame
comb0 <- combinations (n, k)
comb1 <- combinations (n, k-1)
comb2 <- combinations (n, k-2)
left0 <- apply (comb0, 2, function (x, expl) paste(expl[x], collapse = " +
   "), expl)
left1 <- apply (comb1, 2, function (x, expl) paste(expl[x], collapse = " +
   "), expl)
left2 <- apply (comb2, 2, function (x, expl) paste(expl[x], collapse = " +
   "), expl)
left3 <- "1"
form <- c(paste("resp ~ ", left0), paste("resp ~ ", left1), paste("resp ~
   ", left2), paste("resp ~ ", left3))
form
for (i in seq(along = form))
{
   out2[i,] <- c(form[i])
   out1[i,] <- c(glm(formula = form[i], family = poisson)["df.residual"]
   [[1]], extractAIC(glm(formula = form[i], family = poisson)))
}
out2
out.final <- data.frame (out1, out2)
# makes data frame of outputs
out.final[[3]] <- out.final[[3]] + ((2*(out.final[[2]])*(out.final[[2]] +
   1))/(sample.size - out.final[[2]] - 1))
# changes AIC value to AICc value for small samples
# makes data frame of outputs
out.final

I have 7 dependent variables (say X1, X2 ... X7) and want to run Poisson
regressions on all models with 3 or less dependent variables (63 models by
my calculations).  For each model I want to put the AIC values of the
models into a table so that we can compare all of the AIC values for the
models run.  I am trying to automate this process and was looking for some
guidance on code that will tell S-plus to run all possible models with 3 or
less dependent variables from a set of 7 dependent variables.  I can type
the possible models out, but it just seems there must be a way where I
don't have to do that.  Thanks, Niels
